nodes.label: Theodore I Laskaris
nodes.full: Theodore Laskaris, a son-in-law of Alexios III who had fought at the walls in 1204, fled to Asia Minor, took Nicaea as his base and was crowned emperor in 1208 by the new patriarch Michael Autoreianos; he defeated the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw I, who was killed, at Antioch on the Maeander in 1211, fought the Latin emperor Henry and began the state that was to recover Constantinople.
nodes.src: George Akropolites, Chronike Syngraphe; Michael Angold, A Byzantine Government in Exile (1975); Donald Nicol, The Last Centuries of Byzantium (1972).

nodes.label: John III Vatatzes
nodes.full: John Vatatzes, a son-in-law of Theodore I, defeated the Latins at Poimanenon (1224), took Thrace and Thessalonica from the Epirotes (1246) and the Dardanelles and the European coast, ran the state by a careful management of imperial estates, grain and protectionist trade policy, founded hospitals and schools and was remembered as a saint, the Merciful (eleemon).
nodes.src: Akropolites; Angold 1975; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Michael VIII
nodes.full: Michael Palaiologos, a general of the court who became regent for the child John IV Laskaris in 1258 and was crowned in January 1259, won the battle of Pelagonia in 1259, took Constantinople by his general Alexios Strategopoulos without a fight on 25 July 1261, blinded the boy-emperor in December and founded the dynasty that ruled to 1453; he was excommunicated by the Patriarch Arsenios for the blinding and held the empire together through diplomacy until his death.
nodes.src: Akropolites; Pachymeres, Relations historiques; Deno Geanakoplos, Emperor Michael Palaeologus and the West (1959).

nodes.label: Andronikos II
nodes.full: Andronikos II repudiated his father's union with Rome, reduced the fleet and the army and, in the face of the Turkish advance in Anatolia, hired the Catalan Company in 1303; under him the cultural revival, the Chora and the school of Planudes flourished, and his grandson Andronikos III forced him to abdicate in 1328 after the first civil war.
nodes.src: Pachymeres; Nikephoros Gregoras, Historia Rhomaike; Angeliki Laiou, Constantinople and the Latins (1972).

nodes.label: John VI Kantakouzenos
nodes.full: John Kantakouzenos, the grand domestic and chief minister of Andronikos III, who proclaimed himself emperor at Didymoteichon in 1341 against the regency for John V, won the civil war with Serbian and Turkish help and took Constantinople in February 1347, shared power with John V, issued the Histories as a memoir after his abdication in 1354 and spent his last decades as the monk Joasaph.
nodes.src: John Kantakouzenos, Histories; Donald Nicol, The Reluctant Emperor (1996); Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: John V and Manuel II
nodes.full: John V, who came to the throne at nine, was deposed three times; he turned Catholic in Rome in 1369 and became an Ottoman vassal; his son Manuel II (1391–1425), who as a vassal fought for Bayezid at Philadelphia, held the capital against the siege of 1394–1402, travelled to Venice, Paris and London in 1399–1403 to ask for help and wrote orations and dialogues.
nodes.src: Manuel II, Letters (ed. Dennis, 1977); John Barker, Manuel II Palaeologus (1969); Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: John VIII and Constantine XI
nodes.full: John VIII Palaiologos travelled to Italy with 700 men for the Council of Ferrara–Florence in 1437–1439 and returned with a union that was not accepted at home; his brother Constantine XI, despot of the Morea, was crowned at Mistra in January 1449 and died defending Constantinople on 29 May 1453, the last emperor of the Romans.
nodes.src: Sphrantzes, Chronicon; Doukas; Nicol, The Immortal Emperor (1992).

nodes.label: Epirus
nodes.full: Michael I Komnenos Doukas founded in 1205 a state of Greeks in Epirus, and his half-brother Theodore took Thessalonica from the Latins in 1224 and was crowned emperor there in 1227 by the archbishop of Ohrid, in rivalry with Nicaea; defeated by the Bulgarian tsar Ivan Asen II at Klokotnitsa in March 1230, the Epirote emperors were reduced to a despotate and Thessalonica fell to Nicaea in 1246.
nodes.src: Donald Nicol, The Despotate of Epiros (1957); Akropolites; Angold 1975.

nodes.label: Trebizond
nodes.full: Alexios and David Komnenos, grandsons of Andronikos I with Georgian help, took Trebizond in April 1204, a few weeks before the fall of Constantinople, and founded a state on the south Black Sea coast that claimed the imperial title and survived until 1461 through trade, dynastic marriages with Turkmen and Georgian rulers and tribute to the Mongols and Turks.
nodes.src: Anthony Bryer, The Empire of Trebizond and the Pontos (1980); William Miller, Trebizond: The Last Greek Empire (1926).

nodes.label: Latin Empire
nodes.full: Count Baldwin of Flanders was crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia in May 1204 and was captured and died in Bulgaria in 1205; his brother Henry (1206–1216) held the state together, and his successors Peter and Robert of Courtenay and John of Brienne and Baldwin II, who sold the lead of the roofs and pawned his son, ruled a shrinking territory of the city and Thrace, with a Venetian podestà, until July 1261.
nodes.src: Robert de Clari; Geoffrey de Villehardouin; Henri de Valenciennes; Robert Lee Wolff, ‘The Latin Empire of Constantinople’, in A History of the Crusades vol. 2 (1969).

nodes.label: Achaea and Athens
nodes.full: Frankish knights led by Geoffrey of Villehardouin and William of Champlitte conquered the Morea in 1205–1210 and set up the principality of Achaea, with its barons and its Greek peasants, under the Chronicle of the Morea; Otho de la Roche took Athens and Thebes, and Venice held Modon, Coron, Negroponte and Crete; the duchy of Athens was lost to the Catalans in 1311 at the battle of Halmyros.
nodes.src: Chronicle of the Morea (ed. Schmitt, 1904); Peter Lock, The Franks in the Aegean 1204–1500 (1995); David Jacoby; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Adrianople and Baldwin
nodes.full: Kaloyan, tsar of the Bulgarians, who had been refused an alliance by the crusaders, with a Cuman cavalry feigned flight and surrounded the heavy Latin cavalry at Adrianople on 14 April 1205, took Baldwin prisoner and killed Count Louis of Blois; Baldwin died in captivity and the Latin Empire's first emperor was gone within a year.
nodes.src: Villehardouin 358–370; George Akropolites; Fine, The Late Medieval Balkans (1987).

nodes.label: Recovery of Constantinople
nodes.full: The Nicaean general Alexios Strategopoulos, sent with a small force to watch Constantinople, learned that the Venetian fleet was away and entered through a small gate with the help of local Greeks on the night of 24–25 July 1261, burning the Venetian quarter; Michael VIII entered the city on 15 August through the Golden Gate in a procession and was crowned again in Hagia Sophia.
nodes.src: Pachymeres 2; Akropolites 85; Geanakoplos 1959; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Pelagonia and the Angevins
nodes.full: At Pelagonia in 1259 Michael Palaiologos' army destroyed the combined forces of Epirus, Achaea and Sicily, taking William of Villehardouin prisoner, and for twenty years the empire fought Charles of Anjou, who as king of Sicily and Albania from 1272 prepared an invasion; the attack was checked at Berat in 1281 and ended by the Sicilian Vespers of March 1282, which Byzantine gold had helped to fund.
nodes.src: Akropolites; Pachymeres; Geanakoplos 1959; Steven Runciman, The Sicilian Vespers (1958).

nodes.label: Catalan Company
nodes.full: Andronikos II took on 6,500 Catalan and Aragonese soldiers under Roger de Flor to fight the Turks, and after they had cleared Anatolia in 1304 and Roger de Flor was murdered by the emperor's son Michael IX in April 1305, they devastated Thrace and Macedonia for two years and in 1311 took Athens and Thebes at the battle of Halmyros, where they stayed for seventy years.
nodes.src: Ramon Muntaner, Chronicle; Pachymeres; Laiou 1972; Kenneth Setton, Catalan Domination of Athens (1948).

nodes.label: Palaiologan civil wars
nodes.full: Two civil wars, between Andronikos II and his grandson Andronikos III (1321–1328) and then between the regency for John V and Kantakouzenos (1341–1347), were fought with Serbian, Bulgarian and Turkish allies, among them Umur of Aydın and Orhan; they devastated Thrace and Macedonia, enabled the Serbs to take Macedonia, brought in the Ottomans and bankrupted the state.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos, Histories; Gregoras; Nicol 1996; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Zealots of Thessalonica
nodes.full: In 1342 a movement of artisans, sailors and the poor, led by the Zealots Michael Palaiologos and Andreas Palaiologos, took power in Thessalonica against its aristocracy, killed or exiled many, confiscated church and noble estates and ran the city as a quasi-republic until 1350, when Kantakouzenos' forces put the revolt down; it has been interpreted as a social revolution.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos 3; Demetrios Kydones, Letters; Ihor Ševčenko, ‘Nicolas Cabasilas’ Anti-Zealot Discourse’, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 11 (1957).

nodes.label: Gallipoli and the Maritsa
nodes.full: After an earthquake destroyed the walls of Gallipoli in March 1354 Süleyman Pasha, son of Orhan, occupied the town and started the Ottoman settlement in Europe; Edirne fell to Murad I about 1361–1369, and on the Maritsa on 26 September 1371 the Ottoman army destroyed the Serbian forces of the Mrnjavčević brothers, which brought Macedonia and Bulgaria under Ottoman suzerainty.
nodes.src: Gregoras; Kantakouzenos 4; Kritovoulos; Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002).

nodes.label: Siege by Bayezid
nodes.full: Bayezid I, having built the fort of Anadoluhisarı on the Bosphorus in 1395, blockaded the city for eight years, and Manuel II, who had taken the throne in 1391, begged the West for help, which came only in the form of a crusade ending at Nicopolis in 1396 and the marshal Boucicaut's small force; the siege ended only when Timur broke Bayezid at Ankara in 1402, which gave the city another half-century.
nodes.src: Doukas; Sphrantzes; Barker 1969; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Fall of Constantinople
nodes.full: Mehmed II besieged the city with an army of 60,000–80,000 and 70 guns, among them the great bombard of Orban; its defenders were some 7,000, among them Genoese and Venetians under Giovanni Giustiniani, and on the night of 28–29 May the final assault began in the early hours of 29 May and ended with the death of Constantine XI in the breach; the city was sacked for three days and became the Ottoman capital.
nodes.src: Doukas 38–40; Kritovoulos 1; Barbaro, Diary of the Siege; Steven Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965); Roger Crowley, 1453 (2005).

nodes.label: Varna and the last Morea
nodes.full: The crusade of Władysław III of Poland-Hungary and János Hunyadi ended in the destruction of the army at Varna on 10 November 1444 and the king's death; the Despotate of the Morea under Constantine and his brothers Thomas and Demetrios, who had held out against Murad II, was taken by Mehmed II in 1460, and Mistra surrendered.
nodes.src: Callimachus; Sphrantzes; Imber, The Crusade of Varna (2006); Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Partition of Romania
nodes.full: The treaty of March 1204 between the crusader leaders and Venice, concluded before the sack, provided that the Latin emperor should be chosen by a committee of six Venetians and six Franks, receive a quarter of the empire and the palaces, with Venice and the barons dividing the rest and a Venetian, Thomas Morosini, as patriarch; Venice took three eighths of the empire and the city and the ports of Modon, Coron, Crete and Euboea and the islands of the Aegean as a chain of colonial bases.
nodes.src: Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae (1204); Tafel and Thomas, Urkunden vol. 1; David Jacoby, Studies on the Crusader States and on Venetian Expansion (1989).

nodes.label: Palaiologan fiscal state
nodes.full: The Palaiologan government depended on grants of land, pronoiai, which became hereditary under Michael VIII and Andronikos II, on the revenue of the monasteries and on the customs which fell as the Italians took trade; the empire's army shrank to a few thousand mercenaries and tax revenue by 1348 was a fraction of the twelfth century's, which in effect made the state a city and a few provinces.
nodes.src: Angeliki Laiou, ‘The Byzantine Economy in the Mediterranean Trade System’, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 34–35 (1980–1981); Mark Bartusis, The Late Byzantine Army (1992).

nodes.label: Council of Lyons
nodes.full: To avert Charles of Anjou's attack Michael VIII sent a delegation to the Council of Lyons, which on 6 July 1274 proclaimed the union of the churches on the basis of the papal primacy and the filioque; the union was unpopular in the East, produced the Arsenite schism and persecution of its opponents, and was repudiated by Andronikos II in 1282, after Pope Martin IV, Charles of Anjou's ally, had excommunicated Michael in 1281.
nodes.src: Acts of the Council of Lyons II; Geanakoplos 1959; Pachymeres.

nodes.label: Council of Florence
nodes.full: John VIII, the patriarch Joseph II and some 700 Greeks, among them Bessarion of Nicaea and Mark Eugenikos of Ephesus, went to Ferrara in 1438 and then Florence, and a decree of union Laetentur caeli was signed on 6 July 1439 by all but one of the Greek bishops, Mark of Ephesus; the union was rejected by most Orthodox clergy and people and was not enforced in Constantinople until December 1452.
nodes.src: Acts of the Council of Florence (ed. Gill); Joseph Gill, The Council of Florence (1959); Sphrantzes.

nodes.label: Despotate of the Morea
nodes.full: Kantakouzenos' son Manuel was in 1349 made despot at Mistra, as the first of the semi-autonomous governors, who in the following century were members of the Kantakouzenos and Palaiologos families, and the despotate recovered most of the Peloponnese from the Franks by 1430; it was a centre of Greek culture and the base of the last emperor.
nodes.src: Chronicle of the Morea; Denis Zakythinos, Le despotat grec de Morée (1932); Steven Runciman, Mistra (1980).

nodes.label: Arsenite schism
nodes.full: Patriarch Arsenios excommunicated Michael VIII for the blinding of the boy-emperor in 1261 and was deposed in 1265; his supporters, the Arsenites, who denied the legitimacy of the Palaiologan dynasty, remained a party of opposition among the monks and lay people for half a century, with the union of Lyons as a new cause, and were reconciled in 1310.
nodes.src: Pachymeres 3–5; Nicol 1972; Geanakoplos 1959.

nodes.label: Palamas and hesychasm
nodes.full: Barlaam of Calabria attacked the prayer of the Athonite hesychasts, who claimed to see the divine light of Tabor with the bodily eyes; Gregory Palamas defended it by distinguishing God's inaccessible essence from his energies, which men can share, and the councils of 1341, 1347 and 1351 vindicated his doctrine, which became the dogma of the Orthodox Church; opponents saw in it a rejection of rational theology.
nodes.src: Gregory Palamas, Triads; John Meyendorff, A Study of Gregory Palamas (1964); Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Mistra
nodes.full: The hill city of Mistra in the Peloponnese with the monasteries of Brontochion, the Peribleptos and the Pantanassa and the palace of the despots, whose frescoes are among the finest of the age, was the cultural centre of the late empire, where Plethon taught and where the last despots lived; the city was taken by the Ottomans in 1460.
nodes.src: Runciman, Mistra (1980); Sharon Gerstel (ed.), Viewing the Morea (2013).

nodes.label: Latin church and relics
nodes.full: The Latins installed a Venetian patriarch, Thomas Morosini, a Latin chapter in Hagia Sophia and Latin bishops, and removed many relics, among them fragments of the True Cross and the crown of thorns (sold by Baldwin II to Louis IX in 1238), to Venice, Paris and elsewhere; the Greek patriarch, who lived in exile at Nicaea, crowned the Laskarid emperors.
nodes.src: Wolff 1969; Paul Riant, Exuviae sacrae Constantinopolitanae (1877–1878); Angold 1975.

nodes.label: Chora mosaics
nodes.full: Theodore Metochites, the grand logothete of Andronikos II, rebuilt and decorated the monastery church of the Chora (Kariye) in about 1315–1321, with mosaics of the infancy of Christ and the life of the Virgin, the figure of Metochites offering the church to Christ and a fresco of the Anastasis in the funerary chapel, the most refined work of the Palaiologan Renaissance.
nodes.src: Paul Underwood, The Kariye Djami (1966–1975); Robert Ousterhout, The Art of the Kariye Camii (2002).

nodes.label: Painting of Mistra and Serbia
nodes.full: The frescoes of the Peribleptos at Mistra (c. 1350–1370) and the Serbian royal foundations at Gračanica (1321), Dečani and Ravanica, in a style of lively narrative and expressive figures, were painted by artists from Thessalonica and Constantinople; the artists' work spread the Palaiologan style to the Balkans and Russia, where Theophanes the Greek worked in Novgorod and Moscow.
nodes.src: Sharon Gerstel 2013; Ihor Ševčenko; Doula Mouriki.

nodes.label: Palaiologan Renaissance
nodes.full: The recovery of the capital was followed by a revival of the arts and learning under Andronikos II and the scholar-statesmen, with the collection of the Greek Anthology by Planudes, the poems and letters of Manuel Philes, the romances of chivalry and the vernacular, and the commentaries on Aristotle; the manuscripts copied for the court in its circle are preserved in many libraries.
nodes.src: Nigel Wilson, Scholars of Byzantium (1983); Ihor Ševčenko, ‘The Palaeologan Renaissance’ (1975).

nodes.label: Planudes and Gregoras
nodes.full: Maximos Planudes, a monk, teacher of Greek and Latin and translator of Ovid, Cicero and Augustine into Greek, introduced the Indian numerals in his arithmetic, put together the Greek Anthology and rediscovered Ptolemy's Geography; Nikephoros Gregoras, a polymath, wrote the Roman History and works on astronomy, and proposed a calendar reform in 1324 that was ignored.
nodes.src: Planudes, Letters (ed. Leone, 1991); Gregoras; Wilson 1983.

nodes.label: Chioniades
nodes.full: Gregory Chioniades, a Greek scholar who had studied in Tabriz at the Ilkhanid observatory of Maragha under the Persian astronomers, brought to Trebizond and Constantinople the Zij of Persian astronomy, with its planetary models of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and the Maragha school that later reached Copernicus; the learning was a channel between the Islamic and the Greek science.
nodes.src: George Saliba, A History of Arabic Astronomy (1994); David Pingree, ‘Gregory Chioniades and Palaeologan Astronomy’, Dumbarton Oaks Papers 18 (1964).

nodes.label: Metochites
nodes.full: Theodore Metochites (1270–1332), grand logothete, an astronomer, philosopher and poet, wrote the Miscellanea on every subject and the Stoicheiosis astronomike, an introduction to Ptolemy; his library at the Chora and his pupil Gregoras made him the leading literary patron of the Palaiologan revival, and his fall in 1328 sent him to exile and then to monastic retirement.
nodes.src: Metochites, Semeioseis gnomikai; Ioannis Ševčenko, Études sur la polémique entre Théodore Métochite et Nicéphore Choumnos (1962).

nodes.label: Plethon and Bessarion
nodes.full: George Gemistos Plethon (c. 1355–1452), a teacher at Mistra, advocated the revival of Platonism, an ideal state in the Laws and the Hellenic identity of the Greeks, wrote on the differences between Plato and Aristotle, which provoked a quarrel with George Scholarios, and in 1438–1439 lectured in Florence, where Cosimo de' Medici was inspired to found the Platonic Academy; his pupil Bessarion became a cardinal and the main agent of the transfer of the Greek manuscripts to Italy.
nodes.src: Plethon, Laws; Christopher Woodhouse, George Gemistos Plethon (1986); John Monfasani, Byzantine Scholars in Renaissance Italy (1995).

nodes.label: Venice and Genoa
nodes.full: By the Treaty of Nymphaeum of 1261 Michael VIII gave Genoa trading rights and a quarter at Smyrna and Constantinople and, in 1267, Galata across the Golden Horn; the Genoese came to control the Black Sea trade from Kaffa and Tana, the alum of Phocaea and the grain and the customs of the capital, and by 1348, as Gregoras complained, the customs revenue of Galata exceeded that of Constantinople.
nodes.src: Treaty of Nymphaeum (1261); Laiou 1972; Geanakoplos 1959; Nicol, Byzantium and Venice (1988).

nodes.label: Hyperpyron debased
nodes.full: The gold hyperpyron, which since 1092 had had about 20 carats, was debased by Michael VIII to 15 carats and by 1304 to 11, and then declined further in the fourteenth century, when a silver coin, the stavraton, was introduced in 1367; the Venetian ducat replaced the hyperpyron as the standard Mediterranean money.
nodes.src: Hendy, Coinage and Money in the Byzantine Empire (1969); Morrisson, Byzantine Money (2012); Laiou 1972.

nodes.label: Ruin of the capital
nodes.full: The city, which had fallen to a population of 50,000 to 100,000 by 1400 from 400,000 in the twelfth century, was described by travellers such as Clavijo, Bertrandon de la Broquière and Pero Tafur as a series of villages inside the walls, with abandoned palaces and churches and fields and gardens, and with its trade in the hands of Italians.
nodes.src: Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane (1403–1406); Pero Tafur, Travels and Adventures; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Walls and guns
nodes.full: The triple line of the Theodosian walls, repaired by Manuel II and John VIII and with its towers and moat, had held against the siege engines for a thousand years; in 1453 the Ottoman bombards, above all those cast by Orban, breached the wall at the Mesoteichion and the Charisian Gate, while the defenders used cannon from the walls that damaged their own parapets.
nodes.src: Doukas; Kritovoulos; Barbaro; Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005); Crowley 2005.

nodes.label: Treaty of Nymphaeum
nodes.full: Michael VIII made with Genoa, Venice's rival, a treaty giving Genoese merchants freedom of trade, exemption from all taxes and a quarter in the principal ports of the empire, in return for a fleet of fifty ships to help recover Constantinople; Venice, which had been expelled, recovered its privileges by the treaty of 1268 and the empire became a playground for the two republics.
nodes.src: Treaty of Nymphaeum (13 March 1261); Geanakoplos 1959; Nicol 1988.

nodes.label: Mongols and Mamluks
nodes.full: Michael VIII allied with the Mongol Golden Horde of Berke and the Mamluk sultan Baybars against Charles of Anjou, the Latins and the Ilkhanids, giving the Mamluks passage for their ships, and married his illegitimate daughters, Maria and Euphrosyne, to the Ilkhan Abaqa and the khan Nogai; Anatolia's Turks and the Mongols made the empire's east a zone of vassal states.
nodes.src: Pachymeres; Akropolites; Geanakoplos 1959; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: John V and Manuel II in the West
nodes.full: John V went to Rome in 1369, professed the Catholic faith before Urban V and was detained for debts in Venice on his return; Manuel II, after the French marshal Boucicaut had relieved the city in 1399, went from Venice to Paris and London, where he was received by Charles VI and Henry IV, and collected promises that were not kept.
nodes.src: Barker 1969; Manuel II, Letters; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Ottoman vassalage
nodes.full: After the Maritsa, John V and his sons accepted the position of vassals of Murad I and Bayezid, paying tribute and sending troops to the sultan's campaigns, and Manuel II served at the siege of Philadelphia in 1390; after Ankara the empire recovered Thessalonica and the coasts for a time, but in 1424 Manuel's son John VIII became a tributary of Murad II again and the emperor's power was a city and the Morea.
nodes.src: Doukas; Sphrantzes; Barker 1969; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Black Death
nodes.full: The plague arrived in Constantinople from the Crimea in the spring of 1347, possibly by Genoese ships from Kaffa, and spread over the empire and into the Aegean, killing, in the accounts of Kantakouzenos and Gregoras, a large part of the people, among them Kantakouzenos' own youngest son Andronikos; later outbreaks took the empire's population down further.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Nicol 1972; Dionysios Stathakopoulos, Famine and Pestilence in the Late Roman and Early Byzantine Empire (2004).

nodes.label: Turkish settlement of Anatolia
nodes.full: Turkmen warbands of the Mongol marches took the Byzantine frontier fortresses in Bithynia and the Meander region from the 1280s, and the emirs of Menteshe, Aydın, Saruhan, Karasi and Osman had by about 1340 absorbed all of western Anatolia but the cities of Philadelphia, Nicaea and Nicomedia, which fell in 1326–1337 and, in the case of Philadelphia, in 1390; Greek peasants converted or fled to the coast.
nodes.src: Pachymeres 9–13; Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor (1971); Kafadar, Between Two Worlds (1995).

nodes.label: Albanians in the Morea
nodes.full: Albanian herdsmen and soldiers, invited by the despots of Mistra and by the Franks, came into Thessaly and Greece in the fourteenth century and settled in large numbers in the Peloponnese and Attica, where they kept their language until modern times; the despots also settled Greek refugees from Asia Minor and Thrace.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos; Chronicle of the Morea; Nicol 1972; Fine 1987.

nodes.label: Empresses and learned women
nodes.full: Theodora Raoulaina (c. 1240–1300), niece of Michael VIII, kept a scriptorium, built a monastery and was a patron of manuscripts; Irene Choumnaina Palaiologina, daughter of Nikephoros Choumnos, was a nun who corresponded with Theoleptos of Philadelphia and funded the monastery of Philanthropos; and the empress Anna of Savoy, regent for John V in 1341–1347, led the party opposed to Kantakouzenos, in a society where women could be heads of religious foundations and manuscript owners.
nodes.src: Alice-Mary Talbot, Women and Religious Life in Byzantium (2001); Donald Nicol, The Byzantine Lady (1994).

nodes.label: Genoese of Galata
nodes.full: Galata, a walled Genoese town of some ten thousand people on the north shore of the Golden Horn with its own podestà, council and churches, its warehouses and tower of Christ, was run as a colony with trading links to Kaffa, Chios and Genoa, and the Genoese played both sides in the siege of 1453, officially neutral and unofficially helping the Ottomans.
nodes.src: Laiou 1972; Nicol 1988; Kritovoulos; Barbaro.

nodes.label: Zealots and the poor
nodes.full: The Zealots, with sailors and artisans, drew on the grievances of the poor in the second city of the empire against its great landowners and the officials, as in the writings of Kydones and Kabasilas; their regime has been compared with the communes of Italy, though it is possible they may have been less a class than a political party.
nodes.src: Kydones; Kabasilas; Ševčenko 1957; Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: Jews of the empire
nodes.full: Jewish communities in Constantinople, Thessalonica, Crete, Euboea and elsewhere were diminished but survived under Palaiologan rule and the Italians, as tanners, silk dyers and moneylenders; the Karaite community was in Constantinople, and many families left or moved to Ottoman cities after 1400, with arrivals of Sephardic Jews from the West in the fifteenth century.
nodes.src: Steven Bowman, The Jews of Byzantium (1985); Nicol 1972.

nodes.label: The sack of Constantinople
nodes.full: The crusaders’ capture of the city on 12–13 April 1204 and the division of the empire among Venice and the Latin barons ended the Komnenian state and created the Greek successor states.
nodes.src: background — see the Byzantine Empire 867–1204 folio (byzantine-empire-867-1204)

nodes.label: The rise of the Ottoman state
nodes.full: The Ottoman beylik, founded by Osman on the frontier of Bithynia, grew in the fourteenth century from a Turkmen principality to a power that crossed into Europe and encircled the empire.
nodes.src: background — see the Ottoman Empire 1299–1517 folio (ottoman-empire-1299-1517)
